TMDB movies: exploratory data analysis¶

This notebook explores the cleaned TMDB dataset (~2,500 films) straight from the SQLite database built by src/build_db.py. It answers five questions:

  1. What does the catalogue look like? Size, time span, completeness, distributions.
  2. What drives box office? Budget, genre, release month.
  3. Is money linked to quality? Budget vs rating, popularity vs rating.
  4. Who are the people behind the hits? Directors and actors.
  5. How has film changed over time? Budgets, runtimes and genre mix by decade.

Every chart is saved to reports/figures/ so it can be reused in the README or a report.

In [1]:

1. Load the tables from SQLite¶

In [2]:
raw_movies = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM movies", con, parse_dates=["release_date"])
genres = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT mg.movie_id, g.genre_name FROM movie_genres mg JOIN genres g USING (genre_id)""", con)
directors = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT c.movie_id, p.person_name AS director
    FROM crew_credits c JOIN jobs j USING (job_id) JOIN people p USING (person_id)
    WHERE j.job = 'Director'""", con)
cast = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT c.movie_id, p.person_name AS actor, c.cast_order
    FROM cast_credits c JOIN people p USING (person_id)""", con)

print(f"{len(raw_movies):,} films, {raw_movies.release_year.min()}-{raw_movies.release_year.max()}")

2. Decision: how to handle budget and revenue values of 0¶

The cleaning step deliberately did not change budget or revenue. TMDB records an unknown figure as 0, so a 0 means "we don't know", not "this film was free" or "this film earned nothing". Before any money analysis we need to decide what to do with them. First, how big is the problem?

In [3]:
zero_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "films with 0": [(raw_movies.budget == 0).sum(), (raw_movies.revenue == 0).sum()],
    "share of films": [(raw_movies.budget == 0).mean(), (raw_movies.revenue == 0).mean()],
}, index=["budget", "revenue"])
zero_summary.style.format({"share of films": "{:.1%}"})
Out[3]:
  films with 0 share of films
budget 90 3.6%
revenue 102 4.1%

About 4% of films have an unknown budget or revenue. If we left the zeros in, they would be averaged as real $0 values. Compare the statistics with and without them:

In [4]:
compare = pd.DataFrame({
    "zeros counted as $0": [raw_movies.budget.mean(), raw_movies.budget.median(),
                            raw_movies.revenue.mean(), raw_movies.revenue.median()],
    "zeros treated as unknown": [raw_movies.budget.replace(0, np.nan).mean(),
                                 raw_movies.budget.replace(0, np.nan).median(),
                                 raw_movies.revenue.replace(0, np.nan).mean(),
                                 raw_movies.revenue.replace(0, np.nan).median()],
}, index=["mean budget", "median budget", "mean revenue", "median revenue"])
compare["difference"] = compare["zeros treated as unknown"] / compare["zeros counted as $0"] - 1
compare.style.format({"zeros counted as $0": "${:,.0f}", "zeros treated as unknown": "${:,.0f}",
                      "difference": "{:+.1%}"})
Out[4]:
  zeros counted as $0 zeros treated as unknown difference
mean budget $58,629,664 $60,816,431 +3.7%
median budget $37,500,000 $40,000,000 +6.7%
mean revenue $214,180,100 $223,278,963 +4.2%
median revenue $127,900,000 $136,300,000 +6.6%

Counting zeros as real values understates the typical budget and revenue, and it would make ROI impossible (dividing by a $0 budget) and profit misleading (a film with unknown revenue would look like a total loss). There are also a few non-zero revenues that are clearly data-entry errors:

In [5]:
raw_movies.loc[raw_movies.revenue.between(1, MIN_PLAUSIBLE_REVENUE - 1),
               ["title", "release_year", "budget", "revenue"]]
Out[5]:
title release_year budget revenue
987 High School Musical 2006 4200000 3746
1015 The Lion King 1½ 2004 0 1465
1458 Return 2011 0 8801
1977 The Emoji Movie 2017 50000 216
2401 Damsel 2024 60000000 5000
2435 Society of the Snow 2023 65500000 1281

The Emoji Movie did not gross $216, and *Damsel* did not gross $5,000; these are unit mistakes.

Decision

Case Treatment Why
budget == 0 or revenue == 0 treat as unknown (NaN) TMDB's code for "not reported"
revenue under $10,000 treat as unknown (NaN) implausible for these studio films
profit and ROI only when both values are known avoids divide-by-zero and fake losses
ROI rankings budget ≥ $1M only stops micro-budget films (e.g. Primer, $7k) dominating
the film itself kept it is still valid for rating, genre and people analysis

We don't impute (fill in) the missing values: with 4% missing there is enough data without guessing, and invented budgets would distort ROI. The rule lives in src/financials.py so the dashboard uses exactly the same logic.

In [6]:
movies = apply_unknown_financials(raw_movies)
fin = roi_sample(movies).copy()
print(f"{len(movies):,} films kept | budget known for {movies.budget.notna().sum():,} | "
      f"revenue known for {movies.revenue.notna().sum():,} | "
      f"{len(fin):,} usable for ROI (both known, budget >= $1M)")

2,503 films kept | budget known for 2,413 | revenue known for 2,395 | 2,324 usable for ROI (both known, budget >= $1M)

After applying the decision in section 2, only the financial columns have gaps (about 4-5% of films), and those are exactly the unknown values identified above. Ratings, runtime and dates are complete. Note that vote_count starts at 475, so every film here is well known: this is a sample of popular films, not of all films ever released. That matters for interpreting averages.

4. Distributions¶

In [10]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4))
specs = [("vote_average", "Rating (0-10)", 30), ("runtime", "Runtime (minutes)", 30),
         ("popularity", "Popularity (log scale)", 30)]
for ax, (col, label, bins) in zip(axes, specs):
    data = movies[col]
    if col == "popularity":
        data = np.log10(data.clip(lower=0.01))
        data = data[data >= 0]  # popularity >= 1 (drops 6 near-zero outliers from the view)
        ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{10**v:g}"))
        ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(plt.MultipleLocator(1))
    ax.hist(data, bins=bins, color=BLUE, edgecolor=P["surface"], linewidth=1)
    ax.axvline(data.median(), color=P["ink2"], lw=1)
    ax.set_xlabel(label); ax.set_ylabel("Films")
    ax.set_title(label.split(" (")[0])
    ax.text(data.median(), ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.97, f"  median {movies[col].median():.3g}",
            color=P["ink2"], fontsize=9, va="top")
fig.suptitle("Ratings cluster around 7, runtimes around 110 minutes", x=0.01, ha="left",
             fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
save(fig, "01_distributions", FIGURES_DIR); fig
Out[10]:
  • Ratings are tightly packed (median ≈ 6.9, most films between 6 and 8). The sample is survivor-biased toward films people liked enough to vote on.
  • Runtime is roughly normal around 110 minutes, with a long tail of epics over 3 hours.
  • Popularity is heavily right-skewed, so it is shown on a log scale: a few current releases dominate the raw scores.

5. Budget vs revenue: does spending more earn more?¶

In [11]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
ax.scatter(fin.budget, fin.revenue, s=14, color=BLUE, alpha=0.45, edgecolor="none")
lim = [1e6, 4e9]
ax.plot(lim, lim, color=P["ink2"], lw=1)
ax.text(2.2e8, 1.5e8, "break-even\n(revenue = budget)", color=P["ink2"], fontsize=9)
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(lim); ax.set_ylim(1e5, 4e9)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(money_fmt("M")); ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(money_fmt("M"))
ax.set_xlabel("Budget (log scale)"); ax.set_ylabel("Worldwide revenue (log scale)")
r = np.corrcoef(np.log(fin.budget), np.log(fin.revenue))[0, 1]
ax.set_title("Bigger budgets earn more, but the spread is huge")
subtitle(ax, f"{len(fin):,} films with budget ≥ $1M. Log-log correlation r = {r:.2f}. "
             f"{(fin.revenue < fin.budget).mean():.0%} earned less than they cost.")
for t in ["Avatar", "Paranormal Activity", "John Carter"]:
    row = fin[fin.title == t]
    if len(row):
        ax.annotate(t, (row.budget.iloc[0], row.revenue.iloc[0]), xytext=(6, 4),
                    textcoords="offset points", fontsize=9, color=P["ink"])
save(fig, "02_budget_vs_revenue", FIGURES_DIR); fig
Out[11]:
In [12]:
fin[["budget", "revenue", "vote_average", "popularity", "vote_count", "runtime"]].corr(method="spearman").round(2)
Out[12]:
budget revenue vote_average popularity vote_count runtime
budget 1.00 0.69 -0.21 0.34 0.34 0.26
revenue 0.69 1.00 -0.05 0.48 0.54 0.19
vote_average -0.21 -0.05 1.00 0.34 0.34 0.32
popularity 0.34 0.48 0.34 1.00 0.63 0.23
vote_count 0.34 0.54 0.34 0.63 1.00 0.25
runtime 0.26 0.19 0.32 0.23 0.25 1.00

Budget and revenue are strongly related on a log scale, so the money mostly follows the money. But at any given budget, revenue varies by a factor of 10 or more, so budget alone is a weak predictor of a single film's success. The Spearman (rank) correlations above confirm that revenue tracks vote count (how many people watched) much more than vote average (how good they thought it was).

6. Correlation heatmap¶

In [13]:
cols = {"budget": "Budget", "revenue": "Revenue", "roi": "ROI", "runtime": "Runtime",
        "popularity": "Popularity", "vote_count": "Vote count", "vote_average": "Rating",
        "release_year": "Year"}
corr = fin[list(cols)].rename(columns=cols).corr(method="spearman")
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
div = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("div", [P["series"][7], "#f0efec", P["series"][0]])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6.5))
im = ax.imshow(corr, cmap=div, vmin=-1, vmax=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(corr)), corr.columns, rotation=45, ha="right")
ax.set_yticks(range(len(corr)), corr.index)
ax.grid(False)
for s in ax.spines.values(): s.set_visible(False)
for i in range(len(corr)):
    for j in range(len(corr)):
        v = corr.iloc[i, j]
        ax.text(j, i, f"{v:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5,
                color="#ffffff" if abs(v) > 0.6 else P["ink"])
cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8); cb.outline.set_visible(False)
cb.set_label("Spearman correlation", color=P["ink2"])
ax.set_title("Revenue moves with audience size, not with ratings")
save(fig, "03_correlation_heatmap", FIGURES_DIR); fig
Out[13]:
  • Budget ↔ revenue (strong positive) and vote count ↔ revenue (strong positive): films that reach more people earn more.
  • Rating ↔ budget is slightly negative: expensive films are not rated better; mid-budget and older classics score higher.
  • Year ↔ rating is negative: older films in the sample are rated higher (survivorship: only the classics from the 1950s still attract enough votes to be included).

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6.5), sharey=True)
gs = genre_stats
y = np.arange(len(gs))
axes[0].barh(y, gs.median_revenue, color=BLUE, height=0.7)
axes[0].set_yticks(y, gs.index)
axes[0].xaxis.set_major_formatter(money_fmt("M"))
axes[0].set_title("Median revenue per film")
axes[0].grid(axis="y", visible=False)
axes[1].barh(y, gs.median_roi, color=BLUE, height=0.7)
axes[1].axvline(1, color=P["ink2"], lw=1)
axes[1].set_title("Median ROI (revenue ÷ budget)")
axes[1].xaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0f}×"))
axes[1].grid(axis="y", visible=False)
for ax, col, fmt in [(axes[0], "median_revenue", lambda v: f"${v/1e6:,.0f}M"),
                     (axes[1], "median_roi", lambda v: f"{v:.1f}×")]:
    top = gs[col].idxmax(); i = list(gs.index).index(top)
    ax.text(gs[col].max(), i, "  " + fmt(gs[col].max()), va="center", fontsize=9, color=P["ink"])
fig.suptitle("Animation earns the most per film and returns the most per dollar of the big genres",
             x=0.01, ha="left", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
save(fig, "04_genre_revenue_roi", FIGURES_DIR); fig
Out[15]:

Medians are used instead of means because a handful of billion-dollar hits would otherwise dominate each genre. Animation, Adventure and Family lead on revenue per film because they are big-budget, all-audience releases. Animation also has one of the best typical returns (about 4.2×); only Music (a small group of 46 films) is higher. Horror and Romance earn little per film but return about 4× their budget because they are cheap to make. Westerns, History and Sci-Fi have the weakest typical returns. History, Music and War rate highest.

Out[18]:

Budgets are in nominal dollars (not inflation-adjusted), so part of the rise is inflation. The falling average rating is mostly a selection effect: only the best-remembered older films pass the 475-vote threshold, whereas recent films of every quality are included.

11. Box-office concentration¶

In [23]:
rev = movies.revenue.dropna().sort_values(ascending=False).to_numpy()
cum = np.cumsum(rev) / rev.sum() * 100
pct_films = np.arange(1, len(rev) + 1) / len(rev) * 100
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.5))
ax.plot(pct_films, cum, color=BLUE)
ax.plot([0, 100], [0, 100], color=P["neutral"], lw=1)
i20 = np.searchsorted(pct_films, 20)
ax.plot(20, cum[i20], "o", ms=8, color=BLUE, mec=P["surface"], mew=2)
ax.annotate(f"Top 20% of films earn {cum[i20]:.0f}% of revenue", (20, cum[i20]),
            xytext=(12, -18), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=9.5, color=P["ink"])
ax.text(55, 48, "perfectly even split", color=P["ink2"], fontsize=9, rotation=33)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter()); ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter())
ax.set_xlabel("Films, ranked by revenue"); ax.set_ylabel("Share of total revenue")
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, 102)
ax.set_title("Box office is concentrated in a small number of hits")
save(fig, "10_revenue_concentration", FIGURES_DIR); fig

13. Key findings¶

  1. Revenue follows reach, not quality. Revenue correlates strongly with budget and vote count, and weakly (even slightly negatively) with rating.
  2. Big budgets are not more efficient. Only about 8% of films grossed less than their budget (box office alone, before marketing costs and cinema share). ROI multiples are highest for small films (Paranormal Activity, The Blair Witch Project), while blockbusters deliver the biggest absolute profits.
  3. Genre sets the ceiling. Animation, Adventure and Family earn most per film, and Animation also returns about 4× its budget. Horror and Romance are low-revenue but efficient. History, War and Music rate highest; Westerns and History return the least.
  4. Timing matters. May, June and July releases have the highest median revenue, followed by November and December. September and October releases earn the least.
  5. A few hits dominate. The top 20% of films account for well over half of all box office.
  6. Beware selection bias. Every film has 475+ votes, so older decades contain only well-loved classics. Comparisons across decades say as much about what survives as about how films changed.
